subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: How many major atmospheric circulation cells operate in each hemisphere?
questions.explain: The Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells each operate in both hemispheres.

questions.q: Between which latitudes does the Hadley cell circulate air?
questions.explain: The Hadley cell moves air between the equator and around 30 degrees latitude.

questions.q: At the equator, intense heating causes air to rise. What weather does this typically produce?
questions.explain: Rising air cools and condenses, creating low pressure and high rainfall along the ITCZ.

questions.q: Why are many of the world's major hot deserts found at around 30 degrees latitude?
options: Dry air descends there, creating high pressure
Moist air rises there, creating low pressure
Cold ocean currents bring constant rainfall
questions.explain: At around 30 degrees, subsiding air warms and dries to form arid high-pressure conditions.

questions.q: What is the main role of global atmospheric circulation?
options: To redistribute heat from the equator towards the poles
questions.explain: Circulation transfers surplus heat from the tropics to cooler higher latitudes.

questions.q: In which direction do the trade winds blow?
options: From the subtropical high-pressure belt towards the equator
From the equator towards the poles
From the poles towards 60 degrees latitude
From west to east along the equator
questions.explain: Trade winds blow from the subtropical highs at about 30 degrees back towards the equatorial low.

questions.q: A region lies at about 30 degrees North where dry air is constantly sinking. Which biome is most likely to develop there?
questions.explain: Sinking dry air at around 30 degrees creates the arid high-pressure conditions typical of hot deserts.

questions.q: What is the approximate minimum sea surface temperature needed for a tropical cyclone to form?
questions.explain: Tropical cyclones require ocean temperatures of around 27 degrees Celsius to supply enough energy.

questions.q: Why do tropical cyclones only form over warm oceans?
options: Warm water provides energy through evaporation and latent heat
Warm water strengthens the Coriolis effect
Warm water lowers air pressure at the poles
questions.explain: Evaporation from warm seas releases latent heat that powers the developing cyclone.

questions.q: Why do tropical cyclones not form within about 5 degrees of the equator?
options: The Coriolis effect is too weak to make the storm spin
questions.explain: Near the equator the Coriolis effect is negligible, so a storm cannot begin to rotate.

questions.q: What is the calm, clear centre of a tropical cyclone called?
questions.explain: The eye is the calm central region of descending air, surrounded by the stormy eyewall.

questions.q: What does the Saffir-Simpson scale measure?
options: The intensity of a tropical cyclone based on wind speed
The height of a storm surge only
questions.explain: The Saffir-Simpson scale ranks cyclones from category 1 to 5 by sustained wind speed.

questions.q: Why does a tropical cyclone usually weaken after it makes landfall?
options: It is cut off from its warm, moist ocean energy source
The Coriolis effect increases over land
It gains energy from friction with the land
questions.explain: Over land the cyclone loses the warm ocean moisture that fuels it, so it dissipates.

questions.q: Which location is most likely to experience the formation of a tropical cyclone?
options: An ocean at 28 degrees Celsius located at 15 degrees North
A cool ocean at 19 degrees Celsius located at 45 degrees North
An ocean at 24 degrees Celsius located at 2 degrees North
questions.explain: Cyclones need warm seas of around 27 degrees Celsius and a latitude far enough from the equator for the Coriolis effect.

questions.q: A farming region faces months of below-average rainfall and repeated crop failure. Which adaptation would best help it manage the drought?
questions.explain: Drought-resistant crops help communities adapt to reduced water availability.

questions.q: The Milankovitch cycles describe natural variations in which of the following?
options: The Earth's orbit, axial tilt and wobble
The strength of the trade winds
questions.explain: Milankovitch cycles are changes in eccentricity, axial tilt and precession that alter climate over long timescales.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'enhanced greenhouse effect'?
options: Extra greenhouse gases trap more heat and warm the planet
The natural cooling of the atmosphere by clouds
The reflection of sunlight by ice sheets
The removal of carbon dioxide by the oceans
questions.explain: Human-released greenhouse gases increase heat trapping beyond the natural greenhouse effect.

questions.q: How does burning fossil fuels contribute to climate change?
options: It releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, into the atmosphere
It reduces the amount of methane in the air
questions.explain: Burning coal, oil and gas emits carbon dioxide, strengthening the greenhouse effect.

questions.q: A coastal country builds sea walls to protect towns from rising sea levels. This is an example of which response to climate change?
questions.explain: Adaptation manages the effects of climate change, whereas mitigation reduces its causes.

questions.q: Which of the following provides evidence of past climate change?
questions.explain: Air bubbles trapped in ice cores reveal past temperatures and greenhouse gas concentrations.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Geography B (1GB0) specification; Weather Hazards & Climate Change
